title: VeruSAGE-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Rust System Verification
claim: Our benchmark exercises a much broader and denser range of proof techniques than prior benchmarks, which rarely use them.
layout: single heatmap grid, features as rows, benchmarks as columns, color bar right
description: A single annotated heatmap. Rows are eight Verus proof features: induction, contradiction, assert forall, choose, bit-vector, non-linear, compute, and vstd::arithmetic. Columns are grouped under two headers. The first is VeruSAGE-Bench, with nine project columns (AL, AC, IR, MA, NO, NR, OS, ST, VE) plus a bold All column. The second is Prior benchmarks, with Verus-Bench, HumanEval-Verus and Alpha-Verus, separated from the first group by a thick vertical line. Each cell shows the fraction of task files that use the feature, as a number from 0.00 to 0.67 or so. Cells are colored on a green-yellow-orange-red scale, with a colorbar labeled 'fraction of tasks' on the right. The VeruSAGE-Bench columns are visibly warmer, with orange cells for assert forall, induction and bit-vector. The prior-benchmark columns are mostly green. The eye goes to the orange cells at the left and the bold All column.
caption: Fraction of task files in each benchmark that use selected Verus proof features.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive capability to understand and develop code. However, their capability to rigorously reason about and formally prove the correctness of software systems remains in question. Current benchmarks for formal proof generation focus on isolated tasks, typically algorithmic-style problems utilizing basic data structures. We curate a new benchmark suite for system-level proof generation, VeruSAGE-Bench, which consists of 849 proof tasks extracted from eight open-source Verus-verified Rust systems, covering operating systems, storage systems, memory allocators, and more. These tasks are much more complicated than those in previous benchmarks, containing on average more than 20x the formal specification (in Lines of Code) and requiring a much broader array of verification techniques. We evaluate six LLMs on VeruSAGE-Bench (o4-mini, GPT-5, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Qwen3.5), and demonstrate that different models and agentic setups lead to vastly different success rates and costs. We also show that the best models possess impressive capability in writing correctness proofs and hence should inspire new ways of developing trustworthy software. Meanwhile, some difficult tasks in VeruSAGE-Bench stress even the best model, forcing long reasoning time (over an hour on the hardest tasks, 15.3 min per task on average), high token cost (USD 13.65 per task on average), and proof failures, which we hope will guide future improvements in models and agents. This is particularly true for a harder no-lemma version of VeruSAGE-Bench, where the helper lemmas written by human experts are removed: there, the best model proves only 41% of the tasks from the hardest project, at USD 96 per task.
